headings.text: 3 Position as a function of time

html:
The big picture

Kinematics describes how a body moves without asking why; the why (forces) is dynamics, from 8 Newton's Laws and Forces. A moving body is a mass point whose position vector \vec r(t) changes with time; the change between two moments is the displacement \Delta\vec r, which is not the same as the distance travelled. Velocity is how fast the position vector changes, acceleration how fast the velocity vector changes. Each comes in two versions: an average one over a time interval (a difference quotient like \Delta\vec r/\Delta t) and an instantaneous one (its limit, the derivative: \vec v = \dot{\vec r}, \vec a = \dot{\vec v} = \ddot{\vec r}). Speed is the length of the velocity vector. Because velocity is a vector, an acceleration can change it in two ways: tangential acceleration (along \vec v) changes the speed, orthogonal acceleration (across \vec v) changes the direction, and in general both are present.

1 Kinematics and dynamics

Lecture: board p. 8 (bottom) – p. 9 (top) · Giancoli §2-1

The board: KINEMATICS, "science of motion, but we don't care why it moves", vs DYNAMICS, "we care why it moves". "Why it moves" means forces. Kinematics needs only positions, times and their derivatives, and answers questions like "where is the stone after 2 s?" once you know how it was thrown. Dynamics then explains the motion from the forces (\vec F = m\vec a). The course does kinematics first because dynamics is written in its language.

Throughout, a moving body is a mass point at its center of mass (3 Center of Mass): its size and rotation are ignored, only its position matters.

2 Position, displacement and distance

Lecture: board p. 9 · Giancoli §2-1, §3-6

Every position is measured relative to a reference frame: a chosen origin and axes, fixed to something (the ground, a train). The board draws such a set of axes x, y, z next to a point (x, y, z).

The board groups three words and contrasts them with a fourth:

  • DISPLACEMENT / LOCATION / POSITION → a VECTOR: \vec s, \vec r, \vec p = f(x, y, z), drawn as an arrow to the point (x, y, z).
  • DISTANCE → a SCALAR: e.g. from A to B, 30\ \mathrm{km}.

The three letters are three names the course uses for the same thing: \vec s (German Strecke), \vec r (radius vector, the arrow from the origin), \vec p (point). "= f(x, y, z)" means it is determined by the coordinates of the point: \vec r = (x, y, z)^\top.

In most textbooks, and in exam questions, the grouped words are three different things:

  • the position vector \vec r points from the origin to where the body is;
  • the displacement \Delta\vec r = \vec r_1 - \vec r_0 is the change of position: the straight arrow from the start point to the end point;
  • the distance is the length of the path actually travelled, a scalar (the board's "30 km from A to B").

Walk 70 m east, then 30 m back west: the distance travelled is 100 m, but the displacement (blue arrow, from start to end) is only 40 m east. (Giancoli Fig. 2-4)

The same idea in 2D: along the curved path the body travels the arc length \Delta\ell, while the displacement \Delta\vec r = \vec r_2 - \vec r_1 is the straight arrow between the two points, shorter than the arc. (Giancoli Fig. 3-16)

Common mistake — distance and displacement are the same thing

Drive around a block and back to the start: the distance is the whole loop, but the displacement is \vec 0. Even on a one-way trip the road bends, so the magnitude of the displacement (straight line A → B) is never larger than the distance and usually smaller. In 1D a displacement can be negative (motion towards -x); a distance never is.

3 Position as a function of time

Lecture: board p. 9 · Giancoli §2-1, §3-6

The board: "\vec s, \vec r, \vec p, \ldots change over time: \vec s = f(x, y, z, t)." The coordinates of the point are functions of time:

\vec r(t) = \begin{pmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \\ z(t) \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • \vec r(t) — position vector at time t (m)
  • x(t), y(t), z(t) — its coordinates at that time (m)
  • t — time (s)

Kinematics is the study of these functions. The board's example is a 1D motion, where only x(t) changes:

Board sketch (p. 9): a car on an x-axis at the start, and again further right later. The first car is labelled "t_0 = 0\,\mathrm s, x_0 = 0\,\mathrm m: INITIAL STATE", the second "t_1 = 2\,\mathrm s, x_1 = 50\,\mathrm m".

t_0 = t(0\,\mathrm{s}) = 0\,\mathrm{s}, \qquad t_1 = t(2\,\mathrm{s}) = 2\,\mathrm{s}, \qquad x_0 = x(t = 0\,\mathrm{s}), \qquad x_1 = x(t = 2\,\mathrm{s})
Symbols
  • t_0 — the starting time, t_1 — a later time (s)
  • x(t) — the car's position on the x-axis at time t (m); x_0 = x(t_0), x_1 = x(t_1)
  • index 0 — the initial state: the values at the start of the observation

"t_0 = t(0\,\mathrm s) = 0\,\mathrm s" is a roundabout way of saying "the clock reads 0\,\mathrm s at the first snapshot"; "x_0 = x(t = 0\,\mathrm s)" means "x_0 is the position at that time". Index 0 for the start and 1 for a later moment is the convention for the rest of the course (v_0, s_0, \varphi_0, …). The car's displacement is x_1 - x_0 = 50\,\mathrm m in the time t_1 - t_0 = 2\,\mathrm s.

Unclear (board p. 9 vs your notes)

The lecturer's notes give the car's position at t_1 = 2\,\mathrm{s} as x_1 = 50\,\mathrm{m}; your notes have 5\,\mathrm{m}. The board version (50 m) is used here; nothing else depends on it.

4 Average velocity; velocity and speed

Lecture: board p. 9 (bottom) – p. 10; 2_Kinematics_ctd.pdf p. 1 (Week 2) · Giancoli §2-2, §3-6

The board distinguishes:

  • VELOCITY → \vec v(x, y, z, t), a vector: how fast and in which direction the position changes; it can depend on place and time;
  • SPEED → v, a scalar: only how fast, the magnitude v = \lvert\vec v\rvert (the "drop the arrow" convention from 2 Vectors and Vector Products).

The simplest measure of "how fast" uses only the start and the end of an interval. The average velocity is the displacement divided by the time it took (Week 2, 13 Oct):

\vec v_m = \frac{\vec r(t + \Delta t) - \vec r(t)}{t_2 - t_1} = \frac{\Delta\vec r}{\Delta t}, \qquad \Delta t = t_2 - t_1
Symbols
  • \vec v_m — average velocity over the interval (m/s), a vector; index m for "mean"
  • \vec r(t) — position vector at time t (point A), \vec r(t + \Delta t) — a time \Delta t later (point B) (m)
  • \Delta\vec r — displacement from A to B (m)
  • \Delta t = t_2 - t_1 — length of the time interval (s)

The numerator uses "t" and "t + \Delta t", the denominator "t_1" and "t_2": the same thing with t_1 = t and t_2 = t + \Delta t. Written consistently, \vec v_m = \dfrac{\vec r(t_2) - \vec r(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1}. For the car of section 3: \vec v_m = \frac{50\,\mathrm m}{2\,\mathrm s} = 25\,\mathrm{m/s} in the +x direction.

Board sketch: a curved path (blue) with two points A and B on it, in an x, y, z system; the position vectors \vec r(t) to A and \vec r(t + \Delta t) to B in green; the displacement \Delta\vec r as a dashed green line from A to B; and the average velocity \vec v_m as a red arrow along it.

Why \vec v_m lies along the chord A \to B. By vector subtraction, \vec r(t_2) - \vec r(t_1) is the arrow from the tip of \vec r(t_1) to the tip of \vec r(t_2), from A to B. Dividing by \Delta t > 0 changes only its length (and its unit to m/s), not its direction. So the average velocity knows only the start and end points; the wiggles of the path in between don't enter.

In 1D, on an x–t graph: the average velocity between t_1 and t_2 is the slope \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} of the straight line P_1P_2 (the chord). (Giancoli Fig. 2-10)

Video shown in class (link on the board): Levin1.mp4 (AAU Seafile).

Common mistake — average velocity is not average speed

Tempting: "average velocity = distance travelled ÷ time". But the formula uses the displacement \Delta\vec r. Run one 400 m lap of a track in 80 s: the average speed is 400/80 = 5\,\mathrm{m/s}, but you end where you started, so the average velocity is \vec 0. And an average speed is not the average of the speeds: 6 km at 60 km/h and then 6 km at 30 km/h take 0.1\,\mathrm h + 0.2\,\mathrm h, so the average speed is 12\,\mathrm{km}/0.3\,\mathrm h = 40\,\mathrm{km/h}, not 45 km/h. The slow part lasts longer and counts more.

5 Instantaneous velocity

Lecture: 2_Kinematics_ctd.pdf p. 1 · Giancoli §2-3, §3-6

A speedometer does not show an average over a trip; it shows the velocity at this moment. To get it, make the interval shorter and shorter:

\vec v(t_1) = \lim_{t_2 \to t_1} \frac{\vec r(t_2) - \vec r(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\vec r}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{\vec r}, \qquad \Delta t = t_2 - t_1
Symbols
  • \vec v(t_1) — instantaneous velocity at the moment t_1 (m/s), a vector
  • \lim_{t_2 \to t_1} — let the second time approach the first (so \Delta t \to 0)
  • \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec r}{\mathrm{d}t} — derivative of the position vector with respect to time; \dot{\vec r} — the same, written with a dot (dot = time derivative)

What the limit does, in the picture. Slide B along the path towards A. The interval shrinks, and the chord A \to B gets shorter and turns until it lies along the tangent to the path at A. The quotient neither blows up nor vanishes: a shorter chord is divided by a shorter time. What remains is the velocity at that instant.

The limit on an x–t graph: move P_2 towards P_1 (via P_i); the chord turns until it becomes the tangent at P_1. Its slope is the instantaneous velocity at t_1. (Giancoli Fig. 2-11)

In 2D the result: at every point the velocity vector (\vec v_1, \vec v_2, green) points along the tangent to the path, while the position vectors \vec r_1, \vec r_2 (blue) point from the origin. (Giancoli Fig. 3-18a)

Why this is the derivative. "Difference quotient, then let the interval go to zero" is exactly the definition of the derivative from 3.1 Differential Calculus, applied to \vec r(t). For a vector function it is done component by component:

\vec v = \dot{\vec r} = \begin{pmatrix} \dot x(t) \\ \dot y(t) \\ \dot z(t) \end{pmatrix}, \qquad v = \lvert\vec v\rvert = \sqrt{\dot x^2 + \dot y^2 + \dot z^2}
Symbols
  • \dot x(t) = \frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt} etc. — rate of change of each coordinate (m/s)
  • v — speed, the length of \vec v (m/s)

Since \vec v lies along the tangent, the velocity always points along the path, and its length says how fast the body runs along it. Over a very short interval the path and its chord have the same length, so the instantaneous speed always equals the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity (for averages this was not true). From now on "velocity" means the instantaneous one. In 1D, v = \dot x is the slope of the x–t graph.

Worked example — from average to instantaneous velocity

A body moves with \vec r(t) = \begin{pmatrix} 2t \\ t^2 \end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{m} (t in seconds). Find its velocity at t_1 = 1\,\mathrm{s}.

  1. Average velocity over [1\,\mathrm{s},\, 1\,\mathrm{s} + \Delta t]: the y-component is \frac{(1 + \Delta t)^2 - 1}{\Delta t} = \frac{2\Delta t + \Delta t^2}{\Delta t} = 2 + \Delta t, so \vec v_m = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 + \Delta t \end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{m/s}.
  2. Let the interval shrink: \Delta t = 1\,\mathrm{s} gives (2,\ 3)^\top, 0.5\,\mathrm{s} gives (2,\ 2.5)^\top, 0.1\,\mathrm{s} gives (2,\ 2.1)^\top, 0.01\,\mathrm{s} gives (2,\ 2.01)^\top (all in m/s).
  3. Take the limit (\Delta t \to 0): \vec v(1\,\mathrm{s}) = (2,\ 2)^\top\,\mathrm{m/s}. Differentiating each component gives the same: \dot{\vec r} = (2,\ 2t)^\top, at t = 1: (2, 2)^\top ✓.
  4. Speed: v = \sqrt{2^2 + 2^2}\,\mathrm{m/s} \approx 2.83\,\mathrm{m/s}.

6 Acceleration

Lecture: 2_Kinematics_ctd.pdf p. 1 · Giancoli §2-4, §3-6

Velocity can change too, and acceleration measures how fast. The construction is the same one level up: replace "position" by "velocity".

Average acceleration:

\vec a_m = \frac{\vec v(t_2) - \vec v(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1} = \frac{\Delta\vec v}{\Delta t}
Symbols
  • \vec a_m — average acceleration over the interval (m/s²), a vector
  • \vec v(t_1), \vec v(t_2) — velocity vectors at the two times (m/s)
  • \Delta\vec v = \vec v(t_2) - \vec v(t_1) — change of the velocity vector (m/s); \Delta t = t_2 - t_1 (s)

Board sketch: \vec v(t_1) and \vec v(t_2) drawn from the same point; \Delta\vec v closes the triangle from the tip of \vec v(t_1) to the tip of \vec v(t_2); a small red arrow \vec a_m along \Delta\vec v.

To subtract two vectors, draw them from the same point; the difference is the arrow from the tip of \vec v(t_1) to the tip of \vec v(t_2) (check: \vec v(t_1) + \Delta\vec v = \vec v(t_2), tip to tail). \vec a_m points the same way as \Delta\vec v, because dividing by \Delta t > 0 doesn't change the direction. In the sketch the two velocities have about the same length but different directions, and there is still a \Delta\vec v: turning is an acceleration too.

Instantaneous acceleration:

\vec a = \lim_{t_2 \to t_1} \frac{\vec v(t_2) - \vec v(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\vec v}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{\vec v} = \ddot{\vec r}
Symbols
  • \vec a — instantaneous acceleration (m/s²), a vector
  • \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec v}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{\vec v} — derivative of the velocity with respect to time
  • \ddot{\vec r} — second derivative of the position (two dots = differentiated twice)

Since \vec v = \dot{\vec r}, differentiating \vec v once more is differentiating \vec r twice; units: m → m/s → m/s². The whole chain is

\vec r(t) \;\xrightarrow{\ \mathrm d/\mathrm dt\ }\; \vec v(t) \;\xrightarrow{\ \mathrm d/\mathrm dt\ }\; \vec a(t)

and 5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion and Free Fall runs it backwards with integrals. In 1D, a = \dot v is the slope of the v–t graph.

The same construction one level up, on a v–t graph: the chord's slope is the average acceleration over \Delta t, the tangent's slope at P_1 the instantaneous acceleration at t_1. (Giancoli Fig. 2-17)

Common mistake — "negative acceleration means slowing down"

In 1D the sign of a only says which way the velocity changes. A car moving towards -x and getting faster has v < 0 and a < 0; a car moving towards -x and braking has v < 0 and a > 0. The body slows down when \vec a points against \vec v, speeds up when it points with \vec v, whatever the signs. Also, a body can have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration: a stone at the top of its throw.

A car moving to the left and braking: both velocities are negative (v_1 = -15, v_2 = -5\,\mathrm{m/s}), but the acceleration a (orange) points to the right, opposite to the motion, so a > 0 here. (Giancoli Fig. 2-16)

Worked example — acceleration from the same motion

For \vec r(t) = (2t,\ t^2)^\top\,\mathrm{m} from section 5:

  1. Velocity: \vec v(t) = \dot{\vec r} = (2,\ 2t)^\top\,\mathrm{m/s}.
  2. Differentiate again: \vec a(t) = \dot{\vec v} = (0,\ 2)^\top\,\mathrm{m/s^2}, constant.
  3. Check with the average acceleration over [1\,\mathrm{s}, 3\,\mathrm{s}]: \vec v(3) - \vec v(1) = (2, 6)^\top - (2, 2)^\top = (0, 4)^\top\,\mathrm{m/s}, divided by 2\,\mathrm{s} gives (0,\ 2)^\top\,\mathrm{m/s^2} ✓ (average = instantaneous here because \vec a is constant).

7 Tangential and orthogonal acceleration

Lecture: 2_Kinematics_ctd.pdf p. 1 · Giancoli §3-6, §5-5

Because \vec v has a length and a direction, an acceleration can change either. The board names the cases:

  • Tangential acceleration: \vec a \parallel \vec v. Sketch: a short arrow \vec v_1, then a longer arrow \vec v_2 on the same line.
  • Orthogonal acceleration: \vec a \perp \vec v.
  • General: combination of both!

What each case does:

  • Tangential (\vec a along the line of \vec v): the velocity keeps its direction and only its length changes, exactly the sketch. Speeding up in a straight line is tangential; so is braking, with \vec a pointing against \vec v (still parallel).
  • Orthogonal (\vec a \cdot \vec v = 0): the push is sideways. The speed stays the same and the direction turns, as in a car taking a bend at a steady 50 km/h.
  • General: any acceleration splits into a part along \vec v and a part across it, with the scalar product from 2 Vectors and Vector Products. With the unit vector of the direction of motion \hat v = \vec v/\lvert\vec v\rvert:
\vec a_\parallel = (\vec a \cdot \hat v)\,\hat v, \qquad \vec a_\perp = \vec a - \vec a_\parallel, \qquad \vec a = \vec a_\parallel + \vec a_\perp
Symbols
  • \hat v — unit vector along \vec v (dimensionless; needs \vec v \neq \vec 0)
  • \vec a \cdot \hat v — signed length of the "shadow" of \vec a on the line of motion (m/s²): positive when speeding up, negative when braking
  • \vec a_\parallel — the tangential part (m/s²); \vec a_\perp — the orthogonal part (m/s²)

The first formula is "shadow length × direction"; the second says "whatever is left must be across". The tangential part changes the speed; the orthogonal part changes the direction.

Why does only the part of \vec a along \vec v change the speed?

Write the squared speed as a scalar product and differentiate with the product rule:

\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\lvert\vec v\rvert^2 = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,(\vec v \cdot \vec v) = 2\,\vec v \cdot \vec a

Symbols: \lvert\vec v\rvert^2 = v^2 — squared speed (\mathrm{m^2/s^2}); \vec v \cdot \vec a — scalar product of velocity and acceleration (\mathrm{m^2/s^3}).

If \vec a \perp \vec v, the scalar product is 0, so the speed does not change; only the component of \vec a along \vec v contributes.

Worked example — splitting an acceleration into its two parts

Same motion, \vec r(t) = (2t,\ t^2)^\top\,\mathrm{m}, at t = 1\,\mathrm{s}: \vec v = (2,\ 2)^\top\,\mathrm{m/s}, \vec a = (0,\ 2)^\top\,\mathrm{m/s^2}.

  1. Unit vector of the motion: \lvert\vec v\rvert = 2\sqrt2\,\mathrm{m/s}, so \hat v = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,(1,\ 1)^\top (45^\circ up and to the right, the tangent of the path there).
  2. Tangential part: \vec a \cdot \hat v = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,(0 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 1)\,\mathrm{m/s^2} = \sqrt2\,\mathrm{m/s^2} \approx 1.41\,\mathrm{m/s^2}, positive, so speeding up. As a vector: \vec a_\parallel = (1,\ 1)^\top\,\mathrm{m/s^2}.
  3. Orthogonal part: \vec a_\perp = \vec a - \vec a_\parallel = (0,\ 2)^\top - (1,\ 1)^\top = (-1,\ 1)^\top\,\mathrm{m/s^2}.
  4. Check: \vec a_\perp \cdot \vec v = (-1)\cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 2 = 0 ✓, and (1,\ 1)^\top + (-1,\ 1)^\top = \vec a ✓.
  5. Read the result: \vec a_\perp points to the left of the direction of motion, so the path bends to the left (upwards), as the parabola y = x^2/4 does.
  6. Cross-check with the speed itself: \lvert\vec v\rvert(t) = 2\sqrt{1 + t^2} has the slope \dfrac{2t}{\sqrt{1 + t^2}} = \sqrt2\,\mathrm{m/s^2} at t = 1\,\mathrm s, exactly \vec a \cdot \hat v: the tangential part is the rate of change of the speed.

Left: the path with \vec v (blue), \vec a (orange), \vec a_\parallel (green, on the line of \vec v) and \vec a_\perp (violet) at t = 1\,\mathrm{s}. Right: the speed over time; the slope of the green line at t = 1\,\mathrm{s} equals the tangential part.

Common mistake — "no acceleration while turning"

A body going round a circle at constant speed is accelerating: its velocity vector keeps changing direction, so \dot{\vec v} \neq \vec 0 even though \lvert\vec v\rvert is constant. The acceleration is then purely orthogonal to \vec v (7 Rotational Kinematics and Circular Motion).

Problem-solving steps — from a position function to velocity and acceleration
  1. Write \vec r(t) as a column of functions of t.
  2. Differentiate each component: \vec v = \dot{\vec r}; again: \vec a = \dot{\vec v}. For averages over an interval, use the difference quotients instead.
  3. Insert the asked time only after differentiating.
  4. Speed: v = \lvert\vec v\rvert. Speeding up or slowing down: sign of \vec a \cdot \vec v.
  5. If asked, split \vec a: \vec a_\parallel = (\vec a \cdot \hat v)\,\hat v, \vec a_\perp = \vec a - \vec a_\parallel; check \vec a_\perp \cdot \vec v = 0.
  6. Check units: m, m/s, m/s².
Connection

The limit and the derivative are the ones from the math prep course: 3.1 Differential Calculus › Limits. The prep physics course had velocity and acceleration only on a line (1 Kinematics); here they are vectors.
